title: Free Practice Test 1
passage:
Dear Dev,

I know it's been far too long since I last wrote — nearly a year, I think, since your wedding. I've been meaning to tell you about the rather dramatic turn my life has taken, and a proper letter feels more fitting than a quick text.

Back in March, I finally did the thing we used to joke about at university: I quit my job at the accounting firm. Fifteen years of spreadsheets was enough. I'd been feeling restless for a while, and after my father passed away last winter, I realized I didn't want to spend another decade in a grey office tower. So I handed in my notice, sold the condo, and moved out to Elk Falls, a small town about three hours north of the city.

Here's the part that'll really surprise you: I've bought a small orchard. Twelve acres of apple and pear trees, plus a crumbling old farmhouse that needs more work than I'd like to admit. The previous owners let it slide, so my first summer has been all ladders, pruning, and learning from my neighbours, who have been endlessly patient with my questions. Just last week, one of them spent an entire afternoon teaching me how to tell when the pears are finally ready to pick. I won't pretend it's been easy — I've never been so tired, or so sunburnt — but I haven't once missed the commute.

The best surprise is how much I enjoy the quiet. Do you remember that camping trip in second year, when we got hopelessly lost and slept under the stars? It feels a little like that, every single day.

Anyway, the real reason I'm writing: the farmhouse has a spare room, and the guest bed is finally assembled. You and Priya should come out for a weekend this autumn, once the harvest is in. There's a cider festival in town that you'd both enjoy, and the drive up here is beautiful at this time of year. Let me know if you can make it.

Your friend,
Marcus

passage:
Dear Ms. Fournier,

I am writing to apply for the position of Visitor Services Assistant at the Harborview Maritime Museum, which was advertised on your website last week. I believe my experience and enthusiasm make me a strong fit for your team.

For the past three years, I have worked as a front-desk associate at the Lakeside Community Centre, where I greeted visitors, answered enquiries, and managed bookings for events and programs. In that role I learned to stay calm and helpful even when the lobby was crowded, and I regularly received positive feedback from guests. Last year I helped introduce a new online booking system and trained several colleagues to use it, which noticeably reduced waiting times at the desk. I am confident all of these skills would transfer well to a busy museum reception.

Beyond my work experience, I have a genuine passion for local history. I completed a diploma in Museum Studies at Riverside College last spring, and for two summers I volunteered as a tour guide at the restored Fairview Lighthouse. Leading those tours taught me how to make historical information engaging for visitors of every age, from restless school groups to curious retirees. I found that people remember a place far better when a guide brings its stories to life, and I would relish the chance to do the same for the museum's collection of ships, charts, and old photographs.

I am available to start immediately and can work weekends and evenings, which I understand are your busiest periods. I am also comfortable with booking and point-of-sale software, having used similar systems at the community centre every day. I am punctual and reliable, and I genuinely enjoy helping the public, even at the busiest times.

Thank you for considering my application. I have attached my résumé and two references, and I would welcome the chance to discuss how I could contribute to the Harborview team. I can be reached by email or phone at any time.

Sincerely,
Rosa Delgado

Read the following passage.

A. The peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) is a cosmopolitan raptor celebrated as the fastest animal on Earth. In its hunting dive, or stoop, it can exceed 300 kilometres per hour. An apex aerial predator, it feeds almost entirely on other birds, which it strikes in mid-flight with a clenched foot. Historically the species inhabited every continent except Antarctica, nesting on high cliff ledges and, occasionally, on tall built structures. Long prized by falconers for its speed and trainability, the peregrine's broad distribution and adaptability made it, until the middle of the twentieth century, a familiar sight across much of North America and Eurasia.

B. In the decades after the Second World War, peregrine populations collapsed across much of their range. Investigators eventually attributed the decline to DDT, a synthetic pesticide that concentrated in the birds' tissues as it moved up the food chain, a process termed bioaccumulation. The compound disrupted the females' calcium metabolism, causing them to lay abnormally thin-shelled eggs that cracked beneath the incubating parent. Reproduction all but ceased. By the early 1970s the peregrine had been extirpated from the entire eastern United States and was regarded as endangered throughout its former territory — a startling reversal of fortune for so widespread and capable a bird.

C. The prohibition of DDT in the early 1970s removed the principal threat, yet the depleted populations could not recover unaided. Conservationists therefore launched ambitious captive-breeding programmes, rearing chicks in incubators and returning them to the wild through hacking, a centuries-old falconry method in which fledglings are gradually acclimatized from an elevated release box. Over roughly two decades, several thousand captive-bred birds were introduced across the continent. The undertaking proved remarkably effective: by 1999 the species had rebounded sufficiently for authorities to remove it from the United States endangered-species list, an outcome few observers had thought possible a single generation earlier.

D. One of the peregrine's most dependable modern strongholds is, improbably, the city. Skyscrapers imitate the sheer cliff ledges the birds instinctively favour, and urban districts teem with pigeons, a plentiful year-round prey. Breeding pairs now raise their young on office towers, bridges, and cathedral spires in dozens of cities, frequently observed by webcams that have turned the falcons into unlikely local celebrities. Some biologists caution that urban living carries hazards of its own, chiefly collisions with glass and traffic, which kill many young birds in their first year. Even so, few dispute that the peregrine's rescue ranks among the signal achievements of twentieth-century conservation.

E. Not given in any of the above paragraphs.

Read the following passage.

A. Tea is an infusion made from the leaves of the evergreen shrub Camellia sinensis, and after water it is the most widely consumed beverage on Earth. Its use is thought to have begun in south-western China, where the plant grows wild. By the Tang dynasty, roughly twelve centuries ago, tea drinking had spread throughout China and had been transformed from a bitter medicinal tonic into a refined social ritual. Scholars composed treatises on its cultivation and preparation, and potters crafted specialized bowls and pots for its service. From China the custom gradually spread to neighbouring Japan and Korea, where it developed its own distinctive ceremonies.

B. Tea reached Europe only in the seventeenth century, carried by Dutch and Portuguese merchants. It arrived as an expensive luxury, taxed heavily and stored in locked caddies. In Britain it soon became a national obsession, and the demand it created reshaped global commerce: swift clipper ships raced across the oceans to deliver the season's first crop, and the tea trade helped finance the expansion of vast commercial empires. So valuable was the leaf that the taxes placed on it helped provoke political unrest, and smuggling flourished wherever duties were high. Whole trade routes were built around satisfying the world's growing thirst.

C. All true tea comes from the same species; the differences among green, black, oolong, and white tea arise entirely from how the picked leaves are processed. After harvesting, the leaves may be withered, rolled, and allowed to oxidize to varying degrees before being dried. Green tea is heated quickly to halt oxidation, preserving its colour and fresh flavour, while black tea is fully oxidized, producing a darker, stronger infusion. The finest teas are still gathered by hand, a slow and labour-intensive practice, and the character of any tea depends heavily on the altitude, soil, and climate of the garden in which it was grown.

D. Tea has long been credited with health benefits, and modern research has examined the high concentration of antioxidant compounds, called polyphenols, that it contains; some studies associate these with modest benefits for the heart. Tea also contains caffeine, though generally less than an equivalent cup of coffee. Today tea is a global industry worth many billions of dollars, cultivated on plantations from Kenya to Sri Lanka and consumed in forms ranging from delicate ceremonial infusions to sweetened iced drinks and convenient teabags. Yet for all its modern commercialization, the simple act of brewing a cup remains, for millions of people, a daily moment of pause.

E. Not given in any of the above paragraphs.

Read the following article.

The town council is weighing a proposal to replace the grass playing fields at Riverside Park with artificial turf, and residents are sharply divided.

The proposal's strongest advocate is Dana Okonkwo, the town's recreation director. She argues that natural grass simply cannot keep up with demand. "Every spring the fields are closed for weeks because they are too wet, and by August they are worn down to dirt," she says. "A turf field can be played on from morning to night, in almost any weather, without needing time to recover." Okonkwo estimates that turf would roughly triple the available playing hours, easing a chronic shortage that currently forces some youth teams to practise on gravel lots or in the next town over. She adds that turf requires no watering, mowing, or fertilizer, which she says would save the town thousands of dollars a year and conserve water during increasingly dry summers.

Not everyone is persuaded. Helen Voss, a parent and member of a local environmental group, worries the plan trades one problem for several new ones. "On a hot day, a turf field can be twenty degrees warmer than grass — hot enough to burn a child's hands," she says. Voss also points to the tiny rubber pellets used as infill, which wash into storm drains and nearby creeks, and to the expense of replacing the entire surface every eight to ten years. "Grass repairs itself. It just grows back," she says. "We should be fixing the drainage, not paving over a park."

Okonkwo counters that modern infill materials are far cleaner than the recycled-tire crumb used a decade ago, and that better drainage alone would never solve the capacity problem. Voss remains unconvinced, noting that "cleaner is not the same as clean." Ravi Mehta, who coaches two youth soccer teams, sees merit on both sides. "My players would love a field that is always open," he admits, "but I do wonder what we are putting under their feet." The council will hold a public consultation before its vote in the spring.

Read the following article.

The Meadowvale School Board is considering pushing the start of the high-school day back by an hour, from 8:15 to 9:15 a.m., and the proposal has divided the community.

Its leading champion is trustee Dr. Aisha Kamara, who points to a growing body of research on adolescent sleep. "Teenagers are biologically wired to fall asleep and wake up later than adults," she says. "Forcing them to start school at 8:15 leaves many chronically sleep-deprived, which hurts their learning, their mood, and even their safety on the road." Kamara cites studies in which schools that delayed their start times saw better attendance, higher grades, and fewer car accidents among student drivers. "This is one of the few changes we can make that costs almost nothing and is backed by solid science," she argues. She adds that several nearby districts have already made the change and reported no drop in students' after-school participation.

Others are far less enthusiastic. Marcus Bell, who speaks for a group of working parents, worries about the ripple effects. "A later start sounds lovely until you realize it means a later finish," he says. "Many of us drop our kids at school on our way to work. If the day ends at 4:00 instead of 3:00, after-school jobs, sports practices, and childcare all get squeezed." Bell also notes that bus schedules and the timing of the neighbouring elementary school would have to be completely reworked. He doubts, too, that teenagers would truly use the extra hour for sleep. "If they simply shift their bedtime an hour later, we will have rearranged everyone's lives for nothing," he says.

Kamara responds that the logistical problems, though real, are solvable, and that the health of students has to come first. Bell counters that families, not only students, will bear the cost of the change. Elena Ruiz, a Grade 11 student, sees both sides. "I would love the extra sleep," she admits, "but I would hate to lose my after-school shift." The board will hold several public consultations in the coming weeks before it votes.
